Negative binomial (NB2) regression

Source: R/nbreg.R
nbreg.Rd

Fits the NB2 regression model $$Y_i \sim \mathrm{NB}(\mu_i, \theta), \quad \log\mu_i = x_i^\top\beta + o_i, \quad \mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = \mu_i + \mu_i^2/\theta,$$ by maximum likelihood. The coefficients \(\beta\) are updated by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) with \(\theta\) held fixed, and \(\log\theta\) by Newton-Raphson with \(\beta\) held fixed; the two steps alternate until convergence. No general-purpose optimizer is used. The parameterization is the same as MASS::glm.nb().

Usage

nbreg(formula, data, offset, control = nbreg_control())

Arguments

formula

A model formula such as y ~ x1 + x2. The response must be a vector of non-negative integer counts. offset() terms are allowed.

data

A data frame containing the variables in formula.

offset

Optional offset vector (e.g. log(exposure)), evaluated in data; it is added to any offset() terms in the formula.

control

A list from nbreg_control().

Value

An object of class "nbreg": a list with components

coefficients

Estimated \(\beta\).

vcov

Estimated covariance matrix of \(\hat\beta\).

theta, SE.theta

\(\hat\theta\) and its standard error.

loglik

Maximized log-likelihood.

df

Number of estimated parameters (\(p + 1\)).

fitted.values, linear.predictors

\(\hat\mu_i\) and \(\hat\eta_i\).

iter, converged

Number of outer iterations and convergence flag.

y, offset, nobs

The response, offset, and number of observations.

call, terms, xlevels, contrasts, model

Information used by predict() and other methods.

Details

Standard errors for \(\beta\) are \((X^\top\hat W X)^{-1/2}\) (diagonal), treating \(\theta\) as known, as glm.nb() does; the standard error of \(\hat\theta\) is \(\{-H(\hat\theta)\}^{-1/2}\), where \(H\) is the second derivative of the log-likelihood in \(\theta\).

See also

nbreg_control(), zinbreg()

Examples

# Simulated data with an exposure offset
set.seed(1)
n <- 300
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n), expo = runif(n, 1, 3))
d$y <- rnbinom(n, size = 2, mu = d$expo * exp(0.5 + 0.8 * d$x))
fit <- nbreg(y ~ x, data = d, offset = log(expo))
fit$coefficients
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>   0.3999129   0.8652156 
fit$theta
#> [1] 2.119073
